topic: Dynamics of Rotation: Torque, Work and Rotational Kinetic Energy
title: Where Does the Kick Go? Rotation Explained Simply | Class 11 Physics
description:
A knife sharpener pedals to keep his stone spinning. A child pulls a string to spin a top. And Aarav watches a potter kick a heavy wheel a few times, and it keeps turning for a long time. Where does the work of each kick go, and how much spin does it buy? In this animated lesson for Class 11 Physics (Chapter 6, System of Particles and Rotational Motion) we learn the dynamics of rotation: torque, work, power and rotational kinetic energy.

On a live motion notebook a 20 N push at the rim spins up a wheel on a fixed axle, while the readout tracks torque, angular acceleration, omega, angle and spin energy, and a graph shows energy growing in a straight line with angle. A slow-mo replay freezes mid-push to show why the work in a tiny turn is torque times d theta. We see link by link why a spinning body has kinetic energy 1/2 I omega squared, build W = tau theta, P = tau omega and tau = I alpha step by step, compare a light and a heavy wheel with two pause-and-think questions, and solve a grinding wheel example. Then the exam trap (omega in rpm), an original JEE Main pattern question, a recap card and three questions to check yourself.

Made for NCERT, CBSE, ISC (CISCE) and PUC (Karnataka) Class 11 students, and for JEE Main and NEET preparation.

In this video:
0:00 A push becomes spin: the potter's wheel
0:26 Pushing a cart vs turning a wheel
0:46 Motion notebook: a wheel spun up by a push at the rim
1:16 Pause and think: the push stops
1:32 Slow-mo replay: work in a tiny turn is torque times d theta
2:02 Why spin energy is 1/2 I omega squared, link by link
2:25 The rules of turning in five steps: W = tau theta, P = tau omega, tau = I alpha
3:07 Light vs heavy wheel + pause and think
3:34 Worked example: a grinding wheel
4:13 Exam trap: omega in rpm
4:36 Practice question (JEE Main pattern)
5:21 Recap and three questions to answer

Next episode: Conservation of Angular Momentum. Spin on a chair and pull your arms in: nobody pushes you, yet you speed up. How?
